Given below are two statements :

Statement I : Sucrose is dextrorotatory. However, sucrose upon hydrolysis gives a solution having mixture of products. This solution shows laevorotation.

Statement II : Hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose. Since the laevorotation of glucose is more than the dextrorotation of fructose, the resulting solution becomes laevorotatory.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

[IMG]


$\begin{array}{l} [α]_{D\text{-sucrose}}=+66.5^{\circ },[α]_{D\text{-Glucose}}=+52.5^{\circ } \\ [α]_{D\text{-Fructose}}=-92.4^{\circ } \end{array}$

⇒ Sucrose is dextrorotatory and hydrolysed product is laevorotatory.

Given below are two statements :

Statement I : Phenol on treatment with $\mathrm{CHCl}_{3}$ /aq. KOH under refluxing condition, followed by acidification produces $p$-hydroxy benzaldehyde as the major product and $o$-hydroxy benzaldehyde as the minor product.

Statement II : The mixture of $p$-hydroxybenzaldehyde and $o$-hydroxybenzaldehyde can be easily separated through steam distillation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Phenol with $\mathrm{CHCl}{}_{3}$ and aqueous alkali (Reimer–Tiemann reaction) reacts through dichlorocarbene, which attacks mainly the ortho position of the phenoxide ion; acidification gives salicylaldehyde ($o$-hydroxybenzaldehyde) as the major product and $p$-hydroxybenzaldehyde as the minor product, so Statement I is false.


[IMG]

$o$-Hydroxybenzaldehyde has intramolecular hydrogen bonding and is steam volatile, while $p$-hydroxybenzaldehyde is associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding and is not, so steam distillation separates the two; Statement II is true.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : Benzene is nitrated to give nitrobenzene, which on further treatment with $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COCl}/\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}$ will give 


[IMG]


Statement II : $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group is a $m$-directing, and deactivating group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When benzene is nitrated, it forms nitrobenzene (benzene with a $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group).

Now, Friedel–Crafts acylation ($\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COCl}/\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}$) needs an aromatic ring that is sufficiently reactive to attack the electrophile.

The $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group is a strongly deactivating group. It pulls electron density away from the benzene ring, so the ring becomes much less reactive.

Because of this strong deactivation, nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts acylation with $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COCl}/\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}$.

So, nitrobenzene will not give the shown acylated product under these conditions.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
In the reaction,

$2\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s})+6\mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq})\to 2\mathrm{Al}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})+6\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+3\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$
options: $11.2\mathrm{L}\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ at STP is produced for every mole of HCl consumed.
$33.6\mathrm{L}\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ is produced regardless of temperature and pressure for every mole of Al that reacts.
$67.2\mathrm{L}\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ at STP is produced for every mole of Al that reacts.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the correct statement, look at the coefficients in the balanced chemical equation:

$2\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s})+6\mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq})\to 2\mathrm{Al}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})+6\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+3\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$

This equation tells us that:

$2\text{moles of}\mathrm{Al}$ react with $6\text{moles of}\mathrm{HCl}$.

As a result, $3\text{moles of}\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{gas}$ are produced.

Now let us check the given options one by one.

For Option A, $\mathrm{HCl}$ is present in an aqueous solution, while $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ is a gas. The direct relationship between reacting volumes applies only to gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, not to liquids or aqueous solutions. So, this statement is incorrect.

For Option B, look at the relation between $\mathrm{HCl}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{2}$:

$6\text{moles of}\mathrm{HCl}\text{produce}3\text{moles of}\mathrm{H}_{2}$

For $1\text{mole of}\mathrm{HCl}$ consumed:

$\text{Moles of}\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{produced}=\frac{3}{6}=0.5\text{mol}$

At standard temperature and pressure ($\text{STP}$), $1\text{mole}$ of an ideal gas occupies $22.4\mathrm{L}$. 

The volume of $0.5\text{mole of}\mathrm{H}_{2}$ at $\text{STP}$ is:

$\text{Volume}=0.5\times 22.4\mathrm{L}=11.2\mathrm{L}$

This statement is correct.

For Option C, the volume of a gas always changes with temperature and pressure according to the gas laws. It cannot remain fixed at $33.6\mathrm{L}$ regardless of conditions. So, this statement is incorrect.

For Option D, $2\text{moles of}\mathrm{Al}$ produce $3\text{moles of}\mathrm{H}_{2}$. 

This means $1\text{mole of}\mathrm{Al}$ produces $1.5\text{moles of}\mathrm{H}_{2}$.

At $\text{STP}$, the volume produced would be:

$1.5\times 22.4\mathrm{L}=33.6\mathrm{L}$

Since the option states $67.2\mathrm{L}$, it is incorrect.

The correct choice is Option B.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
As compared with chlorocyclohexane, which of the following statements correctly apply to chlorobenzene?

A. The magnitude of negative charge is more on chlorine atom.

B. The $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond has partial double bond character.

C. $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond is less polar.

D. $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond is longer due to repulsion between delocalised electrons of the aromatic ring and lone pairs of electrons of chlorine.

E. The $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond is formed using $\mathrm{sp}^{2}$ hybridised orbital of carbon.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In chlorobenzene the carbon bonded to Cl is $sp^{2}$ hybridised and the lone pairs of Cl are delocalised into the ring (+R effect); in chlorocyclohexane the carbon is $sp^{3}$ and no such resonance is possible. So E is true.

Resonance gives the C–Cl bond of chlorobenzene partial double bond character (B true), which makes it shorter (169 pm) than in chlorocyclohexane (177 pm), so D is false.

The $sp^{2}$ carbon, having more s character, is more electronegative, and the +R effect moves electron density from Cl to the ring; both reduce the negative charge on Cl (A false) and make the C–Cl bond less polar (C true).

The correct statements are B, C and E.

Hence, the correct option is (A).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The halogen that makes longest bond with hydrogen in HX, has the smallest covalent radius in its group.

Statement II : A group 15 element's hydride $\mathrm{EH}_{3}$ has the lowest boiling point among corresponding hydrides of other group 15 elements. The maximum covalency of that element E is 4 .

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{HF}<\mathrm{HCl}<\mathrm{HBr}<\mathrm{HI}$ (bond length order)

Bond length in $HX$ increases as we go down the halogen group because the size of the halogen atom increases. So the longest $H-X$ bond is in $\mathrm{HI}$.

$\mathrm{F}<\mathrm{Cl}<\mathrm{Br}<\mathrm{I}$ (radius order)

Covalent radius also increases down the group. So iodine has the largest covalent radius, not the smallest. Hence, the halogen that forms the longest bond with hydrogen (iodine) does not have the smallest covalent radius. 

Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.

$\mathrm{PH}_{3}<\mathrm{AsH}_{3}<\mathrm{NH}_{3}<\mathrm{SbH}_{3}<\mathrm{BiH}_{3}$ (Boiling point order)

From this order, the hydride with the lowest boiling point is $\mathrm{PH}_{3}$. So in Statement II, the element $E$ is phosphorus.

Maximum possible covalency of phosphorous is 6

Phosphorus can show a maximum covalency of $6$ (for example, in $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ it shows covalency $5$, and in $\mathrm{PF}_{6}^{-}$ it shows covalency $6$). So the part “maximum covalency of $E$ is $4$” is false. 

Therefore, Statement II is incorrect.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
The energy required by electrons, present in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen atom to be excited to second Bohr orbit is $____$ $\mathrm{J}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$.

Given: $R_{H}=2.18\times 10^{-11}\mathrm{ergs}$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For hydrogen, $E_{n}=-\dfrac{R_{H}}{n^{2}}$ with $R_{H}=2.18\times 10^{-11}\text{erg}=2.18\times 10^{-18}\text{J}$ (as $1\text{erg}=10^{-7}\text{J}$).

Energy needed per atom for the excitation $n=1\to n=2$:

$\Delta E=R_{H}\left (\dfrac{1}{1^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2^{2}}\right )=\dfrac{3}{4}\times 2.18\times 10^{-18}=1.635\times 10^{-18}\text{J}$

The energy is required in $\text{J mol}^{-1}$, so for one mole of atoms:

$\Delta E=1.635\times 10^{-18}\times 6.022\times 10^{23}\approx 9.84\times 10^{5}\text{J mol}^{-1}$

This agrees with $9.835\times 10^{5}\text{J mol}^{-1}$; $1.635\times 10^{-18}$ is the value per atom, not per mole.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
The correct order of the rate of reaction of the following reactants with nucleophile by $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1$ mechanism is :

(Given : Structures I and II are rigid)

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The rate of an $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1$ reaction is set by ionisation, so it follows the stability of the carbocation formed; a carbocation is stabilised only when its carbon can become planar ($sp^{2}$).

(IV) gives $(\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}){}_{3}\mathrm{C}{}^{+}$, whose charge is delocalised over three benzene rings: the most stable cation, so (IV) reacts fastest.

(III) gives the tertiary butyl cation, planar and stabilised by hyperconjugation and the $+I$ effect of three methyl groups.

(I) (1-bromobicyclo[2.2.2]octane) and (II) (1-bromobicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) are bridgehead bromides of rigid cages: the bridgehead carbon cannot flatten, so the cation formed is pyramidal, strained and poorly stabilised, and both react far slower than (III).

The one-carbon bridge in (II) holds the bridgehead much more tightly pyramidal than the two-carbon bridges in (I), so the cation from (II) is the most strained and (II) is the slowest.

$\text{II}<\text{I}<\text{III}<\text{IV}$

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text: Consider the transition metal ions $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+},\mathrm{Cr}^{3+},\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ and all form low spin octahedral complexes. The correct decreasing order of unpaired electrons in their respective d-orbitals of the complexes is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For each ion, first find its $3d$ electron count after losing electrons to form the $3+$ charge.

Since all are low spin octahedral complexes, electrons will first pair up in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals before entering the higher-energy $e_{g}$ orbitals.

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{Co}^{3+}\to 3\mathrm{d}^{6}\Rightarrow \mathrm{t}_{2\mathrm{g}}^{2,2,2}\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{g}}^{0,0},\text{unpaired electron}=0 \\ \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\to 3\mathrm{d}^{5}\Rightarrow \mathrm{t}_{2\mathrm{g}}^{2,2,1}\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{g}}^{0,0}\text{unpaired electron}=1 \\ \mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\to 3\mathrm{d}^{3}\Rightarrow \mathrm{t}_{2\mathrm{g}}^{1,1,1}\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{g}}^{0,0}\text{unpaired electron}=3 \\ \mathrm{Mn}^{3+}\to 3\mathrm{d}^{4}\Rightarrow \mathrm{t}_{2\mathrm{g}}^{2,1,1}\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{g}}^{0,0}\text{unpaired electron}=2 \end{array}$

Now compare the number of unpaired electrons: $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ has $3$, $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$ has $2$, $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ has $1$, and $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ has $0$.

So, the decreasing order of unpaired electrons is: $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}>\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}>\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}>\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
$\mathrm{A}\to$ product (First order reaction).

Three sets of experiment were performed for a reaction under similar experimental conditions:

Run $1\Rightarrow 100\mathrm{mL}$ of 10 M solution of reactant A

Run $2\Rightarrow 200\mathrm{mL}$ of 10 M solution of reactant A

Run $3\Rightarrow 100\mathrm{mL}$ of 10 M solution of reactant $\mathrm{A}+100\mathrm{mL}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ added.

The correct variation of rate of reaction is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a first order reaction, the rate law is:

Rate $=k[\mathrm{A}]$

This means the rate depends only on the concentration of $\mathrm{A}$, not on the total volume taken.

Run 1: $100\mathrm{mL}$ of $10\quad \mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{A}$ is used, so $[\mathrm{A}]=10\mathrm{M}$.

Run 2: $200\mathrm{mL}$ of $10\quad \mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{A}$ is used, but the concentration is still $[\mathrm{A}]=10\mathrm{M}$ (only volume increased, not concentration).

Run 3: $100\mathrm{mL}$ of $10\quad \mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{A}$ is mixed with $100\mathrm{mL}$ of water, so the solution gets diluted to double the volume.

So the new concentration becomes:

$[\mathrm{A}]=\dfrac{10\times 100}{100+100}=5\mathrm{M}$

Since Rate $=k[\mathrm{A}]$, the rates are:

Run 1: Rate $=k(10)$

Run 2: Rate $=k(10)$

Run 3: Rate $=k(5)$

So, the correct variation is:

$\text{Rate}_{1}=\text{Rate}_{2}>\text{Rate}_{3}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text: A 'p'-block element $(\mathrm{E})$ and hydrogen form a binary cation $(\mathrm{EH}_{\mathrm{x}})^{+}$, while $\mathrm{EH}_{3}$ on treatment with $\mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{HgI}_{4}$ in alkaline medium gives a precipitate of basic mercury(II)amido-iodine. Given below are first ionisation enthalpy values $\left (\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\right )$ for first element each from group 13, 14, 15 and 16. Identify the correct first ionisation enthalpy value for element E.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Element $E$ must be nitrogen $(\mathrm{N})$.

The binary cation $(\mathrm{EH}_{x})^{+}$ formed with hydrogen should match a common stable cation. Nitrogen forms the well-known cation $\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}$ (ammonium ion), so here $E=\mathrm{N}$ and $x=4$.

Also, $\mathrm{EH}_{3}$ means $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ (ammonia). In alkaline medium, $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ reacts with $\mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{HgI}_{4}$ to give a precipitate of basic mercury(II)amido-iodine, which is the characteristic test for ammonia. This again confirms $E=\mathrm{N}$.

Now we compare first ionisation enthalpy values for the first elements of groups 13, 14, 15, and 16: $\mathrm{B}$ (group 13), $\mathrm{C}$ (group 14), $\mathrm{N}$ (group 15), and $\mathrm{O}$ (group 16).

Across a period, first ionisation enthalpy generally increases due to increasing effective nuclear charge. Also, $\mathrm{N}$ has a stable half-filled configuration $2p^{3}$, so its first ionisation enthalpy is higher than $\mathrm{O}$.

Therefore, among $\mathrm{B},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{O}$, nitrogen has the highest first ionisation enthalpy. So the correct value corresponds to $\mathrm{N}$ (approximately $1402\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
Consider a solution of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ dissolved in water in a closed container.

Which one of the following plots correctly represents variation of log (partial pressure of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ in vapour phase above water) $[y$-axis $]$ with $\log$ (mole fraction of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ in water) $[x$-axis $]$ at $25^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ ?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
By Henry's law, the partial pressure of $\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}$ above the solution is proportional to its mole fraction $x_{\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}}$ in water,

$p_{\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}}=K_{H}x_{\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}}$

Taking logarithms,

$\log p_{\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}}=\log x_{\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}}+\log K_{H}$

so the plot of $\log p$ ($y$-axis) against $\log x$ ($x$-axis) is a straight line of slope $1$ with intercept $\log K_{H}$ on the $y$-axis.

For $\mathrm{CO}{}_{2}$ in water at $298\text{K}$, $K_{H}=1.67\text{kbar}$ $(1.67\times 10^{8}\text{Pa})$, so $\log K_{H}$ is positive and the line cuts the $y$-axis above the origin.

Plot (A) passes through the origin (that would need $K_{H}=1$), plot (B) falls and plot (D) is horizontal; only plot (C) is a rising straight line with a positive $y$-intercept.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
$\text{Match the LIST-I with LIST-II}$

List-I Reagents
List-II Name of Reaction involving carbonyl compounds

A.
$NH_{2}-NH_{2},KOH$
I.
Tollen's Test

B.
$Ag(NH_{3})_{2}OH$
II.
Clemmensen Reduction

C.
Aq. $CuSO_{4}$, Sodium Potassium tartrate, KOH
III.
Wolff - Kishner Reduction

D.
$Zn-Hg,HCl$
IV.
Fehling's Test

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A reagent is $NH_{2}NH_{2},KOH$ (hydrazine in strong base). This is used to reduce aldehydes/ketones to hydrocarbons by Wolff–Kishner reduction.  

So, A $\to$ III.

B reagent is $Ag(NH_{3})_{2}OH$ (ammoniacal silver nitrate). This gives silver mirror with aldehydes: Tollen’s test.  

So, B $\to$ I.

C reagent is aqueous $CuSO_{4}$ + sodium potassium tartrate (Rochelle salt) + $KOH$; together they form Fehling’s solution, used in Fehling’s test for aldehydes (red $Cu_{2}O$ ppt).  

So, C $\to$ IV.

D reagent is $Zn$–$Hg,HCl$ which reduces carbonyl group to $-CH_{2}-$ in acidic medium: Clemmensen reduction.  

So, D $\to$ II.

Hence the correct matching is:

$A-III,B-I,C-IV,D-II$

Correct option: B.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The Henry's law constant $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is constant with respect to variations in solution's concentration over the range for which the solution is ideally dilute.

Statement II : $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{H}}$ does not differ for the same solute in different solvents.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Statement I: True.  

For an ideally dilute solution, Henry’s law is obeyed:

$p=K_{H}x$

At a fixed temperature, $K_{H}$ remains constant over the concentration range where the solution behaves ideally (i.e., dilute enough).

Statement II: False.  

$K_{H}$ depends on the nature of the gas (solute) and also the nature of the solvent (and temperature). So, for the same solute, $K_{H}$ can be different in different solvents.

Correct option: B (Statement I is true but Statement II is false).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
The correct order of reactivity of $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{Br}$ in methanol with the following nucleophiles is

$\mathrm{F}^{-},\mathrm{I}^{-},\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{O}^{-}$ and $\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{O}^{-}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In methanol, $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{Br}$, a methyl halide, reacts by the $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ mechanism, so the rate follows the nucleophilicity of the attacking anion in this protic solvent.

Methanol hydrogen-bonds most strongly to small anions with a concentrated charge. $\mathrm{F}{}^{-}$ is therefore the most heavily solvated and the weakest nucleophile, while the large, polarisable and weakly solvated $\mathrm{I}{}^{-}$ is the strongest.

$\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{O}{}^{-}$ and $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{O}{}^{-}$ both attack through oxygen. In phenoxide the negative charge is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is a weaker nucleophile than ethoxide, whose charge stays on oxygen.

The delocalised charge of phenoxide is also far less solvated than the charge of the small fluoride ion, so phenoxide remains a better nucleophile than $\mathrm{F}{}^{-}$:

$\mathrm{I}{}^{-}>\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{O}{}^{-}>\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{O}{}^{-}>\mathrm{F}{}^{-}$

Hence, the correct option is (A).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text: Two p-block elements X and Y form fluorides of the type $\mathrm{EF}_{3}$. The fluoride compound $\mathrm{XF}_{3}$ is a Lewis acid and $\mathrm{YF}_{3}$ is a Lewis base. The hybridizations of the central atoms of $\mathrm{XF}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{YF}_{3}$ respectively are
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{XF}_{3}$ acts as a Lewis acid, so it must have an incomplete octet (it can accept an electron pair).

A common p-block fluoride with formula $\mathrm{EF}_{3}$ that is a Lewis acid is $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$.

In $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$, boron forms three $σ$ bonds with fluorine and has no lone pair, so it has only 6 electrons around it. Therefore, it is electron-deficient and behaves as a Lewis acid.

With three bond pairs around boron, the hybridization is $\mathrm{sp}^{2}$.

$\mathrm{YF}_{3}$ acts as a Lewis base, so it must have a lone pair to donate.

A common p-block fluoride with formula $\mathrm{EF}_{3}$ that is a Lewis base is $\mathrm{NF}_{3}$.

In $\mathrm{NF}_{3}$, nitrogen forms three $σ$ bonds with fluorine and has one lone pair, so it can donate that lone pair and behave as a Lewis base.

With four electron pairs (3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair) around nitrogen, the hybridization is $\mathrm{sp}^{3}$.

So, $\mathrm{XF}_{3}=\mathrm{BF}_{3}$ has hybridization $\mathrm{sp}^{2}$ and $\mathrm{YF}_{3}=\mathrm{NF}_{3}$ has hybridization $\mathrm{sp}^{3}$.

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{XF}_{3}=\mathrm{BF}_{3};\mathrm{sp}^{2} \\ \mathrm{YF}_{3}=\mathrm{NF}_{3};\mathrm{sp}^{3} \end{array}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text: A first row transition metal $(\mathrm{M})$ does not liberate $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ gas from dilute HCl .1 mol of aqueous solution of $\mathrm{MSO}_{4}$ is treated with excess of aqueous KCN and then $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{g})$ is passed through the solution. The amount of MS (metal sulphide) formed from the above reaction is $____$ mol.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{Cu}\leftarrow ^{\text{di.}\mathrm{HCl}}$ no reaction

Step 1: Identify the metal $\mathrm{M}$

A first row transition metal that does not liberate $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ gas with dilute HCl is $\mathrm{Cu}$ (copper). So, $\mathrm{M}=\mathrm{Cu}$.

Step 2: Reaction of $\mathrm{MSO}_{4}$ with excess KCN

So $\mathrm{MSO}_{4}$ is $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$. When $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$ is treated with excess aqueous KCN, copper forms a very stable (perfect) cyanide complex.

$\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}\leftarrow ^{\mathrm{KCN}}[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}]^{3-}_{\text{perfect complex}}\leftarrow ^{\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}}$ no sulphide ppt

Step 3: Passing $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ through the solution

Because copper is present as the stable complex $[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}]^{3-}$, free $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are not available in solution. Therefore, $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ cannot precipitate copper sulphide.

Final Answer

No metal sulphide $\mathrm{MS}$ is formed. Hence, the amount of $\mathrm{MS}$ formed is $0$ mol.

text:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II

  
    
      List-I
Thermodynamic Process
      List-II
Magnitude in kJ
    
  
  
    
      
        A. Work done in reversible, isothermal expansion of $2$ mol of ideal gas
        from $2~\mathrm{dm}^{3}$ to $20\quad \mathrm{dm}^{3}$ at $300\mathrm{K}$.
      
      I. $4$
    
    
      
        B. Work done in irreversible isothermal expansion of $1$ mol ideal gas
        from $1~\mathrm{m}^{3}$ to $3~\mathrm{m}^{3}$ at $300\mathrm{K}$
        against a constant pressure of $3~\mathrm{kPa}$.
      
      II. $11.5$
    
    
      
        C. Change in internal energy for adiabatic expansion of a $1$ mol ideal gas
        with change of temperature $=320\mathrm{K}$ and
        $C–_{V}=\frac{3}{2}R$.
      
      III. $6$
    
    
      
        D. Change in enthalpy at constant pressure of $1$ mol ideal gas with
        change of temperature $=337\mathrm{K}$ and
        $C–_{p}=\frac{5}{2}R$.
      
      IV. $7$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Option (A)

This is a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, so we use the NCERT formula for isothermal reversible work:

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{nRT}\ln \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_{2}}{\mathrm{V}_{1}} \\ =\dfrac{-2\times 8.314\times 300}{1000}\times \ln \left (\dfrac{20}{2}\right )\mathrm{kJ} \\ =-11.5\mathrm{kJ} \end{array}$

The negative sign shows work is done by the gas during expansion. The magnitude of work is $11.5\mathrm{kJ}$.

Option (B)

This is an irreversible isothermal expansion against a constant external pressure, so work is calculated by:

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\text{ext}}[\mathrm{V}_{2}-\mathrm{V}_{1}] \\ =-3[3-1] \\ =-6\mathrm{kJ} \end{array}$

The negative sign again means work is done by the gas. The magnitude of work is $6\mathrm{kJ}$.

Option (C)

For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. For any process (including adiabatic), we use:

$\begin{array}{l} \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{v}}\Delta \mathrm{T} \\ =1\times \dfrac{3}{2}\times \dfrac{8.314\times 320}{1000}100\mathrm{kJ} \\ =3.99 \end{array}$

So the change in internal energy comes out to approximately $3.99\mathrm{kJ}$ (about $4\mathrm{kJ}$).

Option (D)

For an ideal gas, enthalpy also depends only on temperature. At constant pressure, we use:

$\begin{array}{ll} \Delta \mathrm{H} & =\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{p}}\Delta \mathrm{T} \\ =1\times \dfrac{5}{2}\times \dfrac{8.314\times 337}{1000}\mathrm{kJ} \\ =7\mathrm{kJ} \end{array}$

So, $\Delta H=7\mathrm{kJ}$.

text: 'A' is a neutral organic compound (M. F : $\mathrm{C}_{8}\mathrm{H}_{9}\mathrm{ON}$ ). On treatment with aqueous $\mathrm{Br}_{2}/\mathrm{HO}^{(-)}$, ' A ' forms a compound ' B ' which is soluble in dilute acid. ' B ' on treatment with aqueous $\mathrm{NaNO}_{2}/\mathrm{HCl}(0-5^{\circ }\mathrm{C})$ produces a compound ' C ' which on treatment with $\mathrm{CuCN}/\mathrm{NaCN}$ produces ' D '. Hydrolysis of ' D ' produces ' E ' which is also obtainable from the hydrolysis of ' A '. ' E ' on treatment with acidified $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ produces ' F '. ' F ' contains two different types of hydrogen atoms. The structure of ' A ' is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A ($\mathrm{C}{}_{8}\mathrm{H}{}_{9}\mathrm{NO}$) is neutral, and $\mathrm{Br}{}_{2}$/$\mathrm{OH}{}^{-}$ converts it into B, which dissolves in dilute acid, i.e. an amine. This is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, so A is a primary amide $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}\mathrm{CONH}{}_{2}$ and B is the toluidine $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$; an N-substituted amide such as $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CONHCH}{}_{3}$ does not give this reaction.

Diazotisation gives C ($\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}\mathrm{N}{}_{2}{}^{+}\mathrm{Cl}{}^{-}$), $\mathrm{CuCN}$ replaces the diazo group by CN to give D ($\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}\mathrm{CN}$), and hydrolysis of D gives the toluic acid E ($\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}\mathrm{COOH}$), the same acid formed by hydrolysis of the amide A.


[IMG]

Acidified $\mathrm{KMnO}{}_{4}$ oxidises the $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ group to COOH, so F is a benzenedicarboxylic acid $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{4}(\mathrm{COOH}){}_{2}$.


[IMG]

The ortho isomer (phthalic acid) has three kinds of H (two pairs of ring H and COOH), the meta isomer (isophthalic acid) has four (H-2, H-4/H-6, H-5 and COOH), and the para isomer (terephthalic acid) has only two (four equivalent ring H and COOH). F is therefore terephthalic acid, so the $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{CONH}{}_{2}$ groups in A are para to each other: A is 4-methylbenzamide.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

The formal charges on the atoms marked as (1) to (4) in the Lewis representation of $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ molecule respectively are


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Formal charge $=$ (valence electrons) $-$ (non-bonding electrons) $-\dfrac{1}{2}$(bonding electrons).

Atom (1), the O of the O–H group with two single bonds and two lone pairs: $6-4-\dfrac{4}{2}=0$.

Atom (2), N with one N=O and two N–O bonds and no lone pair: $5-0-\dfrac{8}{2}=+1$.

Atom (3), the doubly bonded O with two lone pairs: $6-4-\dfrac{4}{2}=0$.

Atom (4), the singly bonded O with three lone pairs: $6-6-\dfrac{2}{2}=-1$.

The formal charges on atoms (1) to (4) are $0,+1,0,-1$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
Sodium fusion extract of an organic compound $(\mathrm{Y})$ with $\mathrm{CHCl}_{3}$ and chlorine water gives violet color to the $\mathrm{CHCl}_{3}$ layer. 0.15 g of $(\mathrm{Y})$ gave 0.12 g of the silver halide precipitate in Carius method. Percentage of halogen in the compound $(\mathrm{Y})$ is

$____$ . (Nearest integer)

(Given : molar mass $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{C}:12,\mathrm{H}:1,\mathrm{Cl}:35.5,\mathrm{Br}:80,\mathrm{I}:127$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Violet colour in the $\mathrm{CHCl}_{3}$ layer on adding chlorine water indicates iodide ion in the sodium fusion extract (chlorine oxidises $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ to $\mathrm{I}_{2}$, which is violet in $\mathrm{CHCl}_{3}$).  

So, the silver halide precipitate in Carius method is $\mathrm{AgI}$.

Calculation of % iodine
Molar mass of $\mathrm{AgI}=108+127=235\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Mass of $\mathrm{AgI}$ obtained $=0.12\mathrm{g}$

Mass of iodine in $0.12\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{AgI}$:

$m(\mathrm{I})=0.12\times \frac{127}{235}=0.06485\mathrm{g}$

Mass of compound $(Y)=0.15\mathrm{g}$

Percentage of iodine:

$%\mathrm{I}=\frac{0.06485}{0.15}\times 100=43.23%$

Nearest integer $=43$

text:
The cycloalkene $(\mathrm{X})$ on bromination consumes one mole of bromine per mole of $(\mathrm{X})$ and gives the product $(\mathrm{Y})$ in which $\mathrm{C}:\mathrm{Br}$ ratio is 3:1. The percentage of bromine in the product $(\mathrm{Y})$ is $____$ %. (Nearest integer)

(Given : molar mass in $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{H}:1,\mathrm{C}:12,\mathrm{O}:16,\mathrm{Br}:80$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Bromination of a cycloalkene (one double bond) consumes 1 mole of $Br_{2}$ per mole of alkene, which means 2 bromine atoms add across the double bond.  

So, product $(Y)$ is a dibromo compound.

Given in $(Y)$, the ratio $\mathrm{C}:\mathrm{Br}=3:1$.

Let number of carbon atoms $=n$.  

Number of bromine atoms $=2$.

So,

$\frac{n}{2}=\frac{3}{1}\Rightarrow n=6$

Hence $(Y)$ has formula:

$\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{10}\mathrm{Br}_{2}$

(since cyclohexene is $\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{10}$ and it adds $Br_{2}$)

Now molar mass of $(Y)$:

Carbon: $6\times 12=72$

Hydrogen: $10\times 1=10$

Bromine: $2\times 80=160$

Total molar mass:

$72+10+160=242\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Percentage of bromine:

$%Br=\frac{160}{242}\times 100\approx 66.12%$

Nearest integer $=66%$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
Dissociation of a gas $\mathrm{A}_{2}$ takes place according to the following chemical reaction. At equilibrium, the total pressure is 1 bar at 300 K .

$\mathrm{A}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌2\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g})$

The standard Gibbs energy of formation of the involved substances has been provided below:

$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Substance} & \Delta \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\circ }/\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ \mathrm{A}_{2} & -100.00 \\ \mathrm{A} & -50.832 \end{array}$

The degree of dissociation of $\mathrm{A}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ is given by $\left (x\times 10^{-2}\right )^{1/2}$ where $x=$

$____$ . (Nearest integer).

[ Given : $\mathrm{R}=8\mathrm{J}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{K}^{-1},\log 2=0.3010,\log 3=0.48$ ]

Assume degree of dissociation is not negligible.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For $\mathrm{A}{}_{2}(\mathrm{g})2\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g})$:

$\Delta G^{\circ }=2\Delta G_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{A})-\Delta G_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{A}_{2})=2(-50.832)-(-100.00)=-1.664\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

$\ln K_{p}=-\dfrac{\Delta G^{\circ }}{RT}=\dfrac{1664}{8\times 300}=0.693$

Since $\ln 2=2.303\times 0.3010=0.693$, $K_{p}=2$.

Starting from 1 mol of $\mathrm{A}_{2}$ with degree of dissociation $α$, the equilibrium moles are $\mathrm{A}_{2}=1-α$ and $\mathrm{A}=2α$, total $1+α$, at total pressure $P=1$ bar:

$K_{p}=\dfrac{p_{\mathrm{A}}^{2}}{p_{\mathrm{A}_{2}}}=\dfrac{\left (\dfrac{2α}{1+α}\right )^{2}P^{2}}{\dfrac{1-α}{1+α}P}=\dfrac{4α^{2}P}{1-α^{2}}$

$2=\dfrac{4α^{2}}{1-α^{2}}\Rightarrow 2-2α^{2}=4α^{2}\Rightarrow α^{2}=\dfrac{1}{3}$

$α=\left (\dfrac{1}{3}\right )^{1/2}=\left (33.3\times 10^{-2}\right )^{1/2}$

So $x=33.3\approx 33$.

Hence, the answer is 33.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift

text:
Consider the following electrochemical cell at 298 K

$\mathrm{Pt}\left |\mathrm{HSnO}_{2}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\right |\mathrm{Sn}(\mathrm{OH})_{6}{}^{2-}(\mathrm{aq})\left |\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\right |\mathrm{Bi}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}(\mathrm{s})|\mathrm{Bi}(\mathrm{s})$.

If the reaction quotient at a given time is $10^{6}$, then the cell EMF $\left (\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}\right )$ is

$____$ $\times 10^{-1}\mathrm{V}$ (Nearest integer).

Given the standard half-cell reduction potential as

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Bi}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}/\mathrm{Bi},\mathrm{OH}^{-}}^{\circ }=-0.44\mathrm{V}\text{and}\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Sn}(\mathrm{OH})_{6}^{2-}/\mathrm{HSnO}_{2}^{-},\mathrm{OH}^{-}}^{\circ }=-0.90\mathrm{V}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
At the anode (left), $\mathrm{HSnO}{}_{2}{}^{-}$ (Sn $+2$) is oxidised to $\mathrm{Sn}(\mathrm{OH}){}_{6}{}^{2-}$ (Sn $+4$):

$\mathrm{HSnO}{}_{2}{}^{-}+3\mathrm{OH}{}^{-}+\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}\longrightarrow \mathrm{Sn}(\mathrm{OH}){}_{6}{}^{2-}+2\mathrm{e}{}^{-}$

At the cathode (right), $\mathrm{Bi}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{3}$ (Bi $+3$) is reduced to Bi:

$\mathrm{Bi}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{3}(\mathrm{s})+3\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}+6\mathrm{e}{}^{-}\longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Bi}(\mathrm{s})+6\mathrm{OH}{}^{-}$

Taking the anode reaction three times gives the cell reaction $3~\mathrm{HSnO}{}_{2}{}^{-}+\mathrm{Bi}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{3}+3\mathrm{OH}{}^{-}+6\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}\longrightarrow 3\mathrm{Sn}(\mathrm{OH}){}_{6}{}^{2-}+2\mathrm{Bi}$ with $n=6$.

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ }-E_{\text{anode}}^{\circ }=-0.44-(-0.90)=0.46\text{V}$

$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }-\dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q=0.46-\dfrac{0.059}{6}\log 10^{6}=0.46-0.059=0.401\text{V}\approx 4\times 10^{-1}\text{V}$

Hence, the answer is 4.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 22nd January Morning Shift
